title: Class Visit Slides
text:
Context
I’m a data librarian at UCLA. I’m giving a guest lecture to a graduate information studies class (IS 262A) on data management and sharing plans (DMPs) and the role of libraries. The audience is master’s students in library and information science. Today is 2026-10-13. The deck was revised from a 2025 version, and I added a slide on 2026 federal policy changes that I most need verified. I did this research with an AI assistant and web search, so any claim may be wrong, stale, misattributed, or too strongly worded. I want you to find those.
Live deck: https://ucla-data-science-center.github.io/class-visit-slides/2026-10-13-is262a-dmp/slides.html The “federal changes” slide is at the #/what-changed-in-federal-dmp-requirements-in-2026 anchor.

title: Class Visit Slides
section: Already decided, please do not relitigate
text:
Already decided, please do not relitigate

The three case studies (Craigslist scraping, drone imagery over tribal land, voter/clinical data linkage) are anonymized composites from UCLA practice. Don’t fact-check the events, only the external facts they cite (Craigslist terms, CARE Principles).
The structure, tone, and slide order are fixed. I only want accuracy and citation checks, plus talking help for one slide.
Deck design, colors, and photos are out of scope except the photo credits listed in Part B (item 21).

title: Class Visit Slides
text:
How to answer
For every item, give one of: VERIFIED (you checked a primary or authoritative source, link it), WRONG (give the correction and source), STALE or SUPERSEDED (say what changed and when), OVERSTATED (give a safer wording), or UNVERIFIABLE (say what you tried). Prefer primary sources (nih.gov, nsf.gov, datacite.org, the organization’s own page) over blog summaries. Give a confidence level (high/medium/low) for each verdict. Quote the exact source wording where a number, date, or title matters. If you cannot browse, say so up front and mark everything from memory as unverified.

title: Class Visit Slides
section: Part A: the “What changed in federal DMP requirements in 2026” slide (highest priority)
text:
Part A: the “What changed in federal DMP requirements in 2026” slide (highest priority)
Slide text, verbatim:

“NSF: starting April 27, 2026, DMSPs are completed as a form in Research.gov instead of uploaded as a two-page PDF.”
“NIH: a simplified, structured DMS Plan format applies to applications submitted for due dates on or after May 25, 2026. It uses mostly yes/no questions, a short limitations section, and a data-type-and-repository table.”
“NIH: starting October 1, 2026, changes to an approved DMS Plan are reported through the RPPR instead of a separate prior-approval request.”
“Structured forms make plans easier to validate. They aren’t automatically a complete machine-actionable DMP, and some in the field warn that funder-specific structured formats could fragment the DMP ecosystem unless they can still interoperate with each other.”

Speaker notes for the slide, verbatim:

“The controlling notice takes precedence over any older page that still describes the two-page PDF upload, check the notice date if a student finds conflicting guidance.”
“NIH’s simplified format came out of a review of over 1,100 submitted DMS Plans that found many ran long and included unnecessary narrative detail. NIH expects active awards to transition to the new reporting approach during FY 2027.”
“The RPPR change retires the old DMS Prior Approval Request module in eRA Commons.”
“The closing point draws on an April 2026 Upstream/FORCE11 piece that’s still the freshest substantive commentary on this as of the lecture date: NSF and NIH each built their own structured format rather than a shared one, and the piece argues for splitting a DMP into a lightweight proposal-stage plan versus a fuller ‘living’ plan maintained post-award.”

Citations used (check that each URL, identifier, title, and date is real and says what I claim):

NSF: “Chapter II.C.2.j(xi): Data Management and Sharing Plan Requirements (PAPPG 24-1, Supplement 2)”, https://www.nsf.gov/policies/document/pappg24-1-supplement-2. Note says it covers “the transition to a Research.gov DMSP tool for proposals submitted on or after April 27, 2026.”
NIH: NOT-OD-26-046 “Simplified Structured Data Management and Sharing Plan Format”, https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-26-046.html
NIH: NOT-OD-26-100 “Reporting Changes to an Approved Data Management and Sharing Plan through the RPPR”, https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-26-100.html
Upstream/FORCE11: “What Is the Future of Data Management Plans?”, published April 15, 2026, https://upstream.force11.org/what-is-the-future-of-data-management-plans/

Specific doubts I want you to run down:

Is the NSF date about proposals submitted on or after April 27, 2026, or the date the tool went live, or something else? Is it a PAPPG supplement, a new PAPPG (e.g. 26-1), or a Dear Colleague Letter? Is “form in Research.gov instead of a two-page PDF” accurate, and does it apply to all NSF programs or only some? Are there exceptions?
Is the NIH “due dates on or after May 25, 2026” date correct, and is the notice number right? Is “mostly yes/no questions, a short limitations section, and a data-type-and-repository table” an accurate description of the format?
Is the “over 1,100 submitted DMS Plans” review real and in the notice? What is the exact number and wording?
Is “active awards transition during FY 2027” in the notices? Exactly what does NIH say about existing awards?
Is the Oct 1, 2026 RPPR date correct? Does the notice say it retires the Prior Approval Request module in eRA Commons, or is that my inference?
Does the FORCE11 piece actually say NSF and NIH built separate structured formats, warn about fragmentation, and propose a lightweight proposal-stage plan vs. a fuller living plan? Who wrote it? Is “still the freshest substantive commentary” defensible, or has something newer and better appeared? Cite anything newer.
Has anything changed since April 2026 that this slide misses (new NSF PAPPG, NIH further notices, OSTP or other agency moves, DOE/NASA/USDA/DOD DMP requirements, the NIH public access policy timeline)? Tell me what a student or the instructor could raise that would embarrass me.

title: Class Visit Slides
section: Part A2: help me talk to that slide
text:
Part A2: help me talk to that slide
After checking, give me:

A corrected version of the slide’s four bullets if any need changing, with the same length and tone.
A 90-second spoken walkthrough I can say aloud, in plain speech for library school students. No hype.
Three questions students are likely to ask, with short, accurate answers and the source to point to.
One sentence on what this means for what a librarian actually does differently in a DMP review now.

title: Class Visit Slides
section: Part B: other facts and citations in the deck
text:
Part B: other facts and citations in the deck
Check each. The bibliography entries are included so you can check title, author, date, and URL.

Harvard research data lifecycle diagram. Credited to Cioffi, Goldman & Marchese, Harvard, CC BY-NC 4.0, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.8076168, “Version 5, published May 25, 2023”. Check authors, title (“Harvard Biomedical Research Data Lifecycle”), version/date, license, and that the six segments (Plan and Design, Collect and Create, Analyze and Collaborate, Evaluate and Archive, Share and Disseminate, Publish and Reuse) with “Store and Manage” at the center match the real diagram.
Craigslist Terms of Use (https://www.craigslist.org/about/terms.of.use/en). I quote the clause “via robots, spiders, scripts, scrapers, crawlers, or any automated or manual equivalent (e.g., by hand)”. Is that the exact current wording? Is it in the Terms of Use, and which section? Does the claim “prohibit automated or manual collection of its content without permission” fairly summarize it? (Also: the screenshot on that slide is craigslist’s Toronto page. Flag if that’s a problem.)
CARE Principles. Slide says Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics (Indigenous data governance). Notes say CARE complements FAIR: “FAIR is about making data usable, CARE is about who has authority over it and who benefits.” Check the expansion and the framing. Name the originating body and source (GIDA / Global Indigenous Data Alliance, Carroll et al. 2020, Data Science Journal) if correct.
FAIR vs. open. Notes say data can be FAIR under restricted access and that “Accessible” means accessible metadata and a clear access mechanism. Verify against the FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) and GO FAIR wording.
DMP IDs. Notes say “A DMP ID is technically a DOI with resourceTypeGeneral set to OutputManagementPlan, available since DataCite schema 4.4.” Check the schema version and field value. Citation: DataCite, “What is a DMP ID?”, https://support.datacite.org/docs/what-is-a-dmp-id
DMPTool and ORCID. Slide says a registered plan gets a persistent DMP ID and can appear as a work on the creator’s ORCID record. Notes say DMPTool updated institutional sign-on and NIH/NSF templates through 2026. Citation: “DMP IDs and Networked Data Management Plans (maDMPs)”, CDL/DMPTool wiki, https://github.com/CDLUC3/dmptool/wiki/DMP-IDs-and-Networked-Data-Management-Plans-(maDMPs). Does the page support these claims? Is the URL real? Does the DMP ID to ORCID works link actually work as I describe?
RDA DMP Common Standard. Citation: https://rda-dmp-common.github.io/RDA-DMP-Common-Standard/ . I claim it is an interoperability model and “doesn’t impose any funder’s specific business rules.” Check the claim, the working group name, and the URL.
OSTrails DMP-IF. I claim the EU OSTrails project “published a standardized API (built on the same RDA standard) in April 2026 for exchanging maDMPs between different institutions’ tools and repositories.” Citation: “OSTrails Data Management Plan Interoperability Framework (DMP-IF) Factsheet”, Zenodo record 19115854, published April 23, 2026, CC BY 4.0. Check that the record exists, the date, the license, and whether the factsheet is a published API or a description of one. Soften my wording if needed.
UCLA Dataverse. “Citable data publication, with both open and restricted-file workflows.” Cited to the re3data.org record https://www.re3data.org/repository/r3d100010703 . Check that the record is UCLA Dataverse and supports both claims.
Dryad. “Curated publication of openly shareable research data, free to UC researchers and archived long-term through Merritt.” Cited to https://cdlib.org/services/uc3/dryad/ . Bib note says Dryad datasets are archived through the “CoreTrustSeal-certified Merritt repository”. Check: is Dryad free to UC researchers (vs. a data publishing charge waived by institutional membership), does Dryad archive through Merritt, and is Merritt CoreTrustSeal certified?
Redivis. “Controlled-access data management and analysis platform, built for data with real privacy or governance constraints.” Cited to https://docs.redivis.com/ . Fair characterization? Does UCLA actually have a Redivis relationship I should be careful about naming?
Merritt. “The UC system’s preservation repository, generally reached through an organizational account or a service like Dryad rather than direct self-service deposit.” Check against CDL’s description of Merritt.
Software Management Plans. Slide: “Some funders go further and require a separate Software Management Plan (SMP) for projects producing substantial code.” Cited to Software Sustainability Institute, “Writing and Using a Software Management Plan”, https://www.software.ac.uk/guide/writing-and-using-software-management-plan . My bib note says “UK EPSRC’s Software for the Future call, NSF SI2” require software be addressed. Check the page says that, and whether NSF SI2 is still current (I believe it was replaced by CSSI) and whether “require a separate SMP” is accurate for any named funder, or whether “some funders” should be softened.
NSF and software. Slide: “NSF’s DMP guidance explicitly lists software alongside data, samples, and other materials as something a plan must address. NIH’s policy covers ‘scientific data,’ but code needed to interpret or reproduce that data usually rides along with it.” Check the NSF PAPPG language and NIH’s definition of scientific data (and that NIH’s policy does not cover software per se).
FAIR4RS. “Introducing the FAIR Principles for Research Software”, Scientific Data 9, 622 (2022), doi 10.1038/s41597-022-01710-x, credited to “FAIR4RS Working Group”, convened by ReSA, FORCE11, and RDA. Check the DOI, article number, the real author list (I think it is Barker et al.), and the convening bodies. Tell me how to cite it correctly.
CITATION.cff vs. CodeMeta. I say CITATION.cff is YAML and both GitHub and Zenodo read it natively, and CodeMeta is JSON-LD and better for registries like Software Heritage or bio.tools and for dependencies/runtime. Cited to “CodeMeta vs CITATION.cff: Software Citation Metadata”, author listed as CASRAI, https://casrai.org/compare/codemeta-vs-citation-cff/ . I’m suspicious of this source (is it real, is CASRAI the right author, is it authoritative?). Replace it with the best primary sources (citation-file-format.github.io, codemeta.github.io, GitHub docs, Zenodo docs, Software Heritage docs) and correct the claims if wrong. Does Zenodo really read CITATION.cff natively, or CodeMeta/.zenodo.json? Does Software Heritage index CodeMeta?
Software Heritage. Notes: “as of 2026 it’s a recognized UN digital public good archiving over 27 billion source files, and every archived object gets a SWHID, a content-derived identifier.” Bib note: “over 27 billion unique source files from 421 million projects”, press release dated January 21, 2026, https://www.softwareheritage.org/2026/01/21/software-heritage-archive-digital-public-good/ . Check the figures, the Digital Public Good designation (by the Digital Public Goods Alliance, and is “UN” the right word?), the date, and the SWHID description.
DOI vs. metadata. Slide: “A DOI identifies and resolves an object. Its metadata describes the object and how it relates to other things. The DOI itself isn’t metadata.” Is that a defensible statement, or too absolute?
PIDs. Glossary: “ROR: Research Organization Registry, a persistent ID for an institution”; “ORCID: a persistent ID for a researcher, not an institution”; “DOI: Digital Object Identifier, a persistent ID for a published object”. Fine?
Library Carpentry DMP101. I credit “Library Carpentry, Data Management Plans (DMP101), 2022, CC BY 4.0”, URL https://librarycarpentry.org/ (the homepage only). Does a Library Carpentry lesson called DMP101 or similar exist? What is its real title, authors, year, license, and URL? I want a citation that points at the right lesson.
Photo credits. Drone: “Quadcopter Drone in flight” by Project Kei, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons, File:Quadcopter_Drone_in_flight.jpg. Ballot box: “Official Ballot Drop Box - District of Columbia Elections - DC” by Tony Webster, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons. Check author, license, and file name against the Commons pages.
Prior version. Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17360886 is my 2025 version of this lecture (Dennis and Jamison). Check that it resolves and the title and authors match.
Uncited bib entry. “Brand Guidelines: Colors”, UCLA Strategic Communications, https://brand.ucla.edu/identity/colors is in the bibliography but unused in the slides. Flag only if the URL is dead.

title: Class Visit Slides
text:
Part C: bibliography hygiene
Across all entries:

Flag any URL that is dead, redirects somewhere unexpected, or is a generic homepage instead of the specific page.
Flag wrong or missing authors, years, titles, and identifiers.
Flag entries where an organization is listed as author but a personal or group author exists.
Say which entries should get a DOI or a more stable URL.
Anything I cite as “Accessed September 2026” that has changed since.

title: Class Visit Slides
text:
Output format

A one-paragraph summary: how many items are verified, wrong, stale, overstated, unverifiable, and the three most important fixes.
A table for Part A and Part B with columns: item, verdict, evidence and source link, confidence, suggested replacement wording (only if not VERIFIED).
Part A2 deliverables (walkthrough, Q&A, one-liner).
A corrected BibTeX block for every entry you changed.
A short list of things you could not check and why.

Do not end with general thoughts. If you are unsure, say so and say what would settle it.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Why data management plans matter

Funders treat DMPs as proposal and reporting documents.
Researchers get more value when they also use them as working plans.
Good plans support reproducibility, ethical practice, and long-term reuse of the work.


Plans change. Data, methods, collaborators, access conditions, and research questions shift over the life of a project. A DMP written once and filed away stops being useful.


Welcome the class and thank the instructor for the invitation. Briefly introduce your current role at UCLA Library (unit name is in flux with the 2026 reorg, confirm your own title and affiliation before class rather than assuming the old Data Science Center name still applies).
Set the tone early: a DMP is not paperwork you write once. The practical framing in this lecture builds on Library Carpentry’s DMP101 module (Bohman et al. 2025).
Prompt: ask students to think of the last time they documented a data workflow, and how specific they actually were.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
The research data lifecycle



Cioffi, Goldman & Marchese, Harvard, CC BY-NC 4.0


Planning shapes every later stage, but a plan has to flex as the project moves through the cycle.
The DMP is the connective document. It links what happens today to what happens after the grant ends.
Notice “Store & Manage” sits at the center, not as one stage among others. Storage and data safety touch every phase, not just one step in the loop.



Ask which stage tends to cause the most trouble for their disciplines. Use this to set up why plans change instead of standing still: new collaborators, a change in method, a repository that turns out not to fit, a funder requirement that shifts mid-project.
Diagram is CC BY-NC 4.0 from Harvard Medical School / Harvard University (Cioffi et al. 2023). Non-commercial classroom use is covered by the license; if this deck is ever repurposed for anything commercial, swap it out first.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Anatomy of a strong plan









Section
What it covers




Data description
Types, formats, and approximate volume


Documentation
Metadata standards, READMEs, data dictionaries


Storage and backup
Where data live during the project, and how they’re protected


Sharing and access
Timelines, access conditions, and licensing or reuse terms











Section
What it covers




Consent and compliance
Privacy, consent, IRB, contractual, and legal constraints


Repository and preservation
Where data land long-term, and how they stay usable


Roles, retention, and cost
Who’s responsible, how long data are kept, and what it costs





Walk through this quickly and connect each row to a real workflow rather than treating it as compliance text.
Keep storage, synchronization, backup, and preservation conceptually distinct: storage is where data live day to day, sync keeps copies consistent across devices, backup protects against loss, and preservation is a longer-term commitment to keep data usable after the project ends. They’re often handled by different tools and different people.
Mention that some funders allow data-management costs to be budgeted directly into a proposal (storage, curation time, repository fees).

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Weak and strong plan language
Sharing






Weak


“Available upon request.”









Strong


“De-identified survey data will be published in UCLA Dataverse under an appropriate reuse license within six months of project end.”





Storage






Weak


“Data will be backed up regularly.”









Strong


“Data are stored on UCLA Box during the project, with version history retained, and archived to the department’s research storage at project close.”






Small phrasing differences reveal whether the researcher has actually thought through logistics. Encourage students to use language that describes concrete actions and named tools rather than intentions.
Two deliberate corrections from earlier versions of this lecture: don’t present CC BY as the automatic license for all data, use “an appropriate reuse license or terms of use,” since the right choice depends on the data and the funder. And don’t promise “nightly backup” for UCLA Box unless you can point to an authoritative UCLA source confirming that. Version history is the claim we can actually stand behind.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
How librarians support researchers

Review and strengthen DMP language before submission.
Map funder and repository requirements to the specific project.
Advise on metadata, formats, identifiers, and licensing.
Point to campus infrastructure and services: UCLA Dataverse, Redivis, Merritt, and others.
Identify issues that need referral, and connect researchers with IRB, privacy, information security, legal, contracts, or tribal authorities.


Librarians usually identify and route compliance questions. They don’t make binding legal, IRB, security, or tribal-governance decisions themselves.


This is a boundary worth stating plainly, since students sometimes assume a librarian’s sign-off carries legal weight it doesn’t. The librarian’s job is to spot the issue early and get it to the right expert, not to adjudicate it.
Also flag that FAIR and open are not synonyms. Data can be FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) under restricted access conditions. “Accessible” in FAIR refers to accessible metadata and a clear access mechanism, not necessarily open access to the data itself.
Transition: “Let’s look at what this support looks like on the ground.”

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
The data interview

Modeled on the reference interview, but focused on data.
Ask early: what formats, what volume, how sensitive, who owns it.
The answers shape both the plan and the project’s long-term access.


This is often the first concrete step a librarian takes with a new project, usually before the DMP itself is drafted. It surfaces storage, sharing, or compliance gaps while there’s still time to change course.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Common problems and librarian interventions

Vague or missing sharing statements → propose a specific repository, timeline, and license.
Weak metadata and documentation → recommend a standard, a README template, a data dictionary.
Unclear storage or backup strategy → separate “where data live” from “how they’re protected.”
Unresolved ethics or consent questions → flag early, route to IRB or privacy office.
Undefined roles → name who deposits, who maintains, who answers questions after the grant ends.


Transition: “Here are three examples from UCLA practice that show how these issues surface in review.” These are anonymized composites drawn from UCLA practice, not independently published case studies, so describe them that way rather than as established external facts.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: Case: scraping Craigslist for housing data
text:
Case: scraping Craigslist for housing data





A project proposed collecting rental listings and landlord contact information to study post-incarceration housing access.
Craigslist’s current terms prohibit automated or manual collection of its content without permission (craigslist, Inc. 2019).
The plan also raised privacy and possible human-subjects questions.
The team paused collection while it reconsidered its method and consulted the appropriate campus offices.



Don’t say a librarian “legally prohibited” or “personally halted” the project. What happened is that librarian review surfaced the terms-of-use conflict early, before the proposal went out, giving the team time to redesign the method.
Craigslist’s Terms of Use prohibit collecting content “via robots, spiders, scripts, scrapers, crawlers, or any automated or manual equivalent (e.g., by hand)” (craigslist, Inc. 2019). Worth reading that clause aloud, students are often surprised manual collection is covered too.
Takeaway: ethical and legal checks belong in every DMP review, not just ones that look sensitive on their face.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: Case: drone imagery over tribal land
text:
Case: drone imagery over tribal land





Quadcopter drone in flight. Photo by Project Kei, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.




A project proposed depositing aerial imagery collected over tribal land in a public repository.
The team recommended pausing the deposit while the researchers consulted the relevant tribal nation and appropriate campus experts.
The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance helped frame questions about collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, and ethics.



Don’t say the librarians “required” CARE. Describe CARE as a governance framework the team used to ask better questions, and as a complement to FAIR rather than a replacement for it: FAIR is about making data usable, CARE is about who has authority over it and who benefits.
Say “the relevant tribal nation,” not a generic “tribal representatives.” Which nation matters, and treating it as interchangeable undercuts the point of the case.
Takeaway: data sovereignty and ethical deposit decisions go hand in hand, and the library’s role here was to slow the process down enough for the right consultation to happen.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: Case: linking voter and clinical data
text:
Case: linking voter and clinical data





Official ballot drop box, Washington, DC. Photo by Tony Webster, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.




A project combined purchased historical voter data (names, addresses) with clinical data from UCLA Health, held under restricted access.
Linking identifiable voter records with clinical information changed the risk profile of the combined dataset.
Review covered the data-use agreement, IRB protocol, consent and permitted uses, access controls, the approved computing environment, and the sharing and retention plan.



Data linkage can make the combined dataset more sensitive than either source considered separately.


Avoid suggesting the problem arose simply because the work crossed disciplines. The issue was the linkage and the resulting identifiability, not the fact that voter data and clinical data came from different fields. Mention how the DMP itself had to be revised once the linkage was proposed, since the original plan didn’t anticipate it.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: What changed in federal DMP requirements in 2026
text:
What changed in federal DMP requirements in 2026

NSF: for proposals submitted on or after April 27, 2026, the DMSP is a form in Research.gov instead of a two-page PDF upload. Data supporting NSF-funded publications must be shared at the time of publication (National Science Foundation 2026).
NIH: a simplified, structured DMS Plan format applies to applications submitted for due dates on or after May 25, 2026. It uses mostly yes/no questions, a short limitations section, and a data-type-and-repository table (National Institutes of Health 2026a).
NIH: starting October 1, 2026, changes to an approved DMS Plan are reported through the RPPR instead of a separate prior-approval request (National Institutes of Health 2026b). Career development (K) awards were exempted from DMS Plan requirements on October 5 (National Institutes of Health 2026c).
Structured forms make plans easier to validate. They aren’t automatically a complete machine-actionable DMP, and some in the field warn that funder-specific structured formats could fragment the DMP ecosystem unless they can still interoperate with each other (Grady and Praetzellis 2026).


The controlling notice takes precedence over any older page that still describes the two-page PDF upload, check the notice date if a student finds conflicting guidance.
NSF’s change is more than a format swap: the revised text also requires sharing the data that support NSF-funded publications at the time of publication, with any exceptions described and justified in the plan (National Science Foundation 2026). Collaborative projects submit one combined plan, and a justified statement that no detailed plan is needed is allowed.
NIH’s simplified format came out of a review of over 1,100 DMS Plans that found many ran long and included unnecessary narrative detail (National Institutes of Health 2026a). Existing awards transition on different routes depending on status: just-in-time review for pending applications, the next RPPR for active awards, and no later than the FY 2027 RPPR (National Institutes of Health 2026b).
The RPPR change (National Institutes of Health 2026b) removes the separate prior-approval requirement for modifying an approved plan, and NIH plans to retire the DMS Prior Approval Request type in the eRA Commons Prior Approval Module. Other award approvals, such as a change in project scope, still apply.
Newest development: on October 5, 2026 NIH exempted career development (K) awards from DMS Plan requirements, effective immediately, for active, pending, and future applications (National Institutes of Health 2026c). So check the award type, not just the date, when a student asks about a particular grant.
Other agencies move on their own schedules (USDA, DOE, and NASA all have their own plans and timelines), so don’t extrapolate the NSF form change to them.
The closing point draws on a March 2026 Upstream/FORCE11 article by Grady and Praetzellis (Grady and Praetzellis 2026): NSF and NIH each built their own structured format rather than a shared one, and the piece argues for splitting a DMP into a lightweight proposal-stage plan versus a fuller “living” plan maintained post-award, which lines up well with the UCLA workflow slide coming up. Present it as their analysis, not as an established finding.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: A UCLA planning and review workflow
text:
A UCLA planning and review workflow



Researcher drafts a funder-specific plan.
Librarian reviews it and identifies questions or referrals.
Project staff implement the storage, documentation, access, and consent commitments.
The plan is updated as methods, data, collaborators, or restrictions change.
Data and related outputs are deposited, preserved, restricted, or disposed of as promised.
The project reports progress and changes to the funder.





Present this as a loop, not a one-way pipeline, step 4 feeds back into steps 1 through 3 continuously over the life of the project, not just once at the start.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
DMPTool demonstration

Log in through UCLA’s institutional single sign-on.
Open a current NIH or NSF template and show how institutional fields populate automatically.
Show the ORCID connection: a registered plan gets a persistent DMP ID and can appear as a work on the creator’s ORCID record.
Show where a plan can link to project outputs, such as a dataset or publication, once they exist.


Keep this under 10 minutes and keep it visual.
Test the exact workflow before class each year, DMPTool has been updating its institutional sign-on and its NIH/NSF templates through 2026, and features can shift. If research-output linking or a specific template field can’t be reliably demonstrated live, use a screenshot instead and say so.
Question for the class: which section do you think most researchers struggle to complete?

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: From a static document to a machine-actionable plan
text:
From a static document to a machine-actionable plan

A conventional DMP is written mainly for a person to read.
A machine-actionable DMP represents key facts in structured fields that systems can exchange, validate, and update: ORCID iDs, RORs, funder and award identifiers, DMP IDs, dataset DOIs, repository identifiers, licenses, access conditions, retention periods, and costs.


Example identifier chain (DataCite, n.d.; California Digital Library, n.d.-a)
Machine-actionable doesn’t mean fully automated. Structured information can reduce repeated data entry and connect systems, but ethical decisions, consent restrictions, and repository suitability still need human judgment.


A DataCite DMP ID is a DOI registered with resourceTypeGeneral set to OutputManagementPlan, supported since DataCite schema 4.4 (DataCite, n.d.). Other identifier types are possible in principle, so say “DataCite DMP ID” when precision matters.
The RDA DMP Common Standard provides the interoperability model behind this (Research Data Alliance DMP Common Standards Working Group, n.d.). Make clear it doesn’t impose any funder’s specific business rules, it’s a shared way to express DMP content, not a policy.
If there’s time, mention that this isn’t just a DMPTool feature: an April 2026 factsheet from the EU’s OSTrails project describes a common REST API and data model (built on the same RDA standard) for exchanging maDMPs between research services (OSTrails 2026). Useful for showing the trend is bigger than one vendor.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
section: Matching data with repositories and services
text:
Matching data with repositories and services

UCLA Dataverse: citable data publication, with both open and restricted-file workflows (re3data.org, n.d.).
Dryad: curated publication of openly shareable research data, no cost to UC researchers through UC’s institutional membership, and archived long-term through Merritt (California Digital Library, n.d.-b).
Redivis: controlled-access data management and analysis platform, built for data with real privacy or governance constraints (Redivis, n.d.).
Merritt: the UC system’s preservation repository, with account-based collections, a deposit interface, and an API. It also sits behind services such as Dryad (California Digital Library, n.d.-c).
Domain repositories, identified through funder or disciplinary guidance, for data with a natural community home.


Distinguish two words students tend to conflate: “sensitive” describes the data and its risks, “restricted” describes an access condition. Marking a dataset restricted doesn’t by itself make sensitive data safe or appropriate to deposit, the sensitivity has to be addressed first.
Don’t imply Merritt is a destination any UCLA researcher can simply walk up to. Access is tied to accounts and collections, and much of its use is as infrastructure other services sit on top of.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Metadata, documentation, and persistent identifiers

Descriptive and disciplinary metadata make a dataset findable and interpretable.
READMEs, data dictionaries, and codebooks explain what’s inside and how it was produced.
Version and provenance notes track how the data changed over time.
Persistent identifiers such as DOIs, ORCID iDs, and RORs identify and resolve people, places, and things.


A DOI identifies an object and resolves to information about it. It is one metadata element, not a substitute for descriptive metadata.


This replaces an older, vaguer framing (“metadata is what turns data into knowledge”) with something more precise: metadata and documentation are what make data interpretable and reusable by someone who wasn’t in the room when it was collected.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Software gets its own treatment

NSF’s sharing requirements include software. NIH’s DMS Policy covers scientific data, while separate NIH guidance encourages sharing research software.
Some funders explicitly require software management planning, within a broader plan or as a separate Software Management Plan (SMP) (Software Sustainability Institute, n.d.).
Give software the same three things data gets:

License: pick one before you publish, don’t leave it implicit.
Identifier and citation: a Zenodo DOI or a Software Heritage SWHID to identify it, and a CITATION.cff file (GitHub reads it natively) to say how to cite it.
Documentation: a README, a dependency list, enough context for someone else to rerun it.



FAIR4RS (2022), a joint RDA/FORCE11/ReSA effort, adapts the FAIR principles specifically for software, since software’s differences from data (it runs, it has versions, it depends on other software) mean the data-FAIR guidance doesn’t map cleanly onto it (Barker et al. 2022).
Two citation-metadata formats come up constantly: CITATION.cff is a YAML file, human-writable, and GitHub reads it directly (GitHub, n.d.; Citation File Format project, n.d.). Zenodo also supports it for GitHub releases, but if a .zenodo.json file is present Zenodo uses that instead (Zenodo, n.d.). CodeMeta is a JSON-LD vocabulary, better suited if the software needs richer descriptive metadata such as dependencies and runtime requirements (CodeMeta Project, n.d.). The choice depends on the workflow.
Software Heritage is worth naming as the software equivalent of a preservation repository. It was recognized as a digital public good by the Digital Public Goods Alliance in January 2026, and reported over 27 billion unique source files from 421 million projects. Archived software artifacts can be cited with a SWHID, a content-derived identifier that doesn’t depend on any single forge (GitHub, GitLab, etc.) (Software Heritage 2026). A SWHID is not a DOI.

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Takeaways, resources, and contact

DMPs work best as living plans, not one-time paperwork.
Librarians identify and route compliance questions. They don’t make binding legal, IRB, security, or tribal-governance decisions.
Structured, machine-actionable plans connect systems, but human judgment still decides what’s ethical and appropriate.

Resources: DMPTool · UCLA Dataverse · re3data.org · FAIRsharing.org
Contact
Tim Dennis, Data Librarian (tdennis@library.ucla.edu)
Jamie Jamison, Data Collections Manager (jamison@library.ucla.edu)
Ashley Peterson, Digital Scholarship Librarian for the Arts & Humanities (ashleypeterson@library.ucla.edu)
Adapted from Library Carpentry DMP101 (CC BY 4.0) (Bohman et al. 2025). 2025 version archived at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17360886 (Dennis and Jamison 2025).

title: Data Management and Sharing Plans and the Role of Libraries
text:
Glossary


DMP: Data Management Plan
DMSP / DMS Plan: Data Management and Sharing Plan (NSF’s and NIH’s specific term for a DMP)
NSF: National Science Foundation
NIH: National Institutes of Health
IRB: Institutional Review Board
DOI: Digital Object Identifier, a persistent, resolvable ID for an object
ORCID: a persistent ID for a person contributing to research, not an institution
ROR: Research Organization Registry, a persistent ID for a research organization

RDA: Research Data Alliance
RPPR: Research Performance Progress Report (an NIH reporting form)
FAIR: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable (data principles, not a synonym for “open”)
CARE: Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics (Indigenous data governance)
maDMP: machine-actionable DMP
SMP: Software Management Plan
SWHID: a Software Heritage identifier for a specific piece of archived code
CC BY / CC BY-NC: Creative Commons license types. BY requires attribution; BY-NC also restricts commercial use.


Not meant to be read aloud. Point students to this slide (and the hoverable <abbr> tags throughout, when viewing on a screen rather than projected) if terminology gets in the way of the discussion.
